title: Transient Memory Smoothing: predictive token throttling and shadow-model warmstart for OOM avoidance
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
GPU OOMs continue to occur at tail under mixed workloads where long-context chat + bursty concurrent requests spike KV cache pressure and combined continuous-batching aggregates push memory over headroom. Current strategies (aggressive eviction, immediate model fallback) are effective but jarring for users: abrupt failures, long cold-start times for fallbacks, and poor latency/quality tradeoffs.

Goal:
Design and implement a multi-stage, low-latency OOM prevention and graceful-recovery flow called 'Transient Memory Smoothing' that reduces OOM incidence and softens user experience when memory is scarce. Key principles: predictive smoothing (anticipate short-term memory pressure), minimally invasive degradation (token-level throttling / progressive shedding), fast warmstart of lower-cost shadow models, and observable, safe retry paths.

Key components (high-level):
1) Predictive Memory Headroom Estimator: lightweight sliding-window predictor per-GPU that consumes batch admission rates, KV footprint delta metrics, and active stream lengths to estimate 0-10s headroom curve. Uses exponentially-weighted moving averages and a small logistic classifier to flag imminent <2s headroom events. No model weights beyond 10k params (on-device heuristics).

2) Token Admission Shaper: fine-grained request admission layer inserted into the batcher. When headroom is predicted to drop below thresholds, admission shaper applies progressive token budgets per request: first trim speculative prefix tokens (low-salience system tokens), then enforce per-request max-token-rate (tokens/sec) and token-budget cap. Shaper signals upstream via standard response headers so SDKs/clients can display degraded mode.

3) Shadow-model Warmstart Pool: maintain a tiny pool of quantized CPU-warm instances (e.g., int4 / 4-bit FP16 hybrid) of selected fallback models kept in a warm-but-evictable state. When severe pressure occurs, requests are diverted to shadow instances rather than eviction-triggered OOMs. Warmstart is opportunistic: pool size adapts to historical fallback rate and cost budget.

4) Progressive Offload Shim: for requests with hot KV segments and long attention windows, attempt speculative partial offload of cold KV pages to CPU with async prefetch back. Offload is probabilistic and measured; if it risks creating CPU bottlenecks we revert.

5) Coordinated Retry & Backoff Policy: if a fallback produces lower-quality output, retry logic allows the original path to attempt again once headroom recovers; retries incorporate jitter and a cap to avoid thrashing. Telemetry ties each retry to originating request for later evals.

Acceptance criteria (must pass to close ticket):
- End-to-end flow implemented in staging serving runtime and feature-flagged.
- Baseline: reduce observed OOM incidents by >= 70% under the targeted stress test (mixed chat + batch spike) without increasing p95 latency by >15%.
- User-visible degradations are annotated: SDK receives headers: 'X-Redwood-Degraded: true' and 'X-Redwood-Mode: token-throttle|shadow-fallback'.
- Warmstart pool maintenance implements cost guardrails and eviction policy; monthly cost delta < 8% for test cluster.
- Telemetry: new dashboards showing headroom predictions, token-throttle events, shadow-fallback rates, retry success rates.

Implementation tasks (rough breakdown):
- T1: Spec for headroom estimator signals, thresholds, and metrics (Aisha) [2d].
- T2: Implement Token Admission Shaper in batcher path (Luca) [5d].
- T3: Shadow-model warmstart pool manager and simple quantized instance image build (infra + runtime) [5d].
- T4: Progressive Offload Shim prototype and safety knobs (runtime eng) [5d].
- T5: Retry orchestration and tracing linkage (platform) [3d].
- T6: End-to-end integration tests and chaos scenarios (SRE) [5d].
- T7: Dashboards & alerts (observability) [3d].
- T8: Docs: SDK headers, expected behaviours, and rollback plan (PM/Docs) [2d].

Rollout plan:
- Canary on a single GPU node pool under feature flag. Monitor headroom predictor accuracy and false-positive throttles for 72 hours.
- Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 75% traffic to nodes with feature enabled, with automated rollback on OOM increase, degraded rate >10% or user-affecting p99 increase.
- Post-rollout: run a 24-hour chaos test that simulates KV-heavy burst patterns to validate graceful degradation.

Observability and SLOs to add:
- OOM-rate (per-GPU, per-minute). Goal: -70% vs baseline after rollout.
- Headroom prediction precision/recall and lead time distribution.
- Token-throttle events per 1k requests.
- Shadow-fallback accept rate and downstream quality delta (BLEU/ROUGE style or endpoint-specific metric).
- Retry success rate and average extra latency.

Risks and mitigations:
- False positives in predictor causing unnecessary throttles: mitigate with conservative thresholds and two-stage confirm (short-term predictor + instantaneous memory check).
- Shadow-model quality gap: pick fallback models tuned for latency/quality tradeoff; expose per-customer config to opt-out.
- CPU/network saturation from offload: cap concurrent offloads and fall back to immediate shadow models if CPU contention detected.

Open questions for architecture review:
- Threshold calculus: fixed headroom seconds vs percentile-based (p95 headroom). Proposal: start with fixed seconds (2s/5s) then refine.
- Shadow-model image format and quantization target: int4 hybrid vs int8? Recommendation: int4 tested for recent evaluation workloads; keep an int8 fallback.
- Billing/telemetry tagging for fallback paths: chargeable as 'shadow-execution' with clear metrics.
